lines.content: Alice is a task manager for people who would rather type than click. She keeps
track of todos, deadlines and events, remembers them between runs, and is
faintly put out about having to do any of it.
She runs either as a JavaFX desktop app, with the conversation on the left and
a live list of your tasks on the right, or as a plain command-line program.
Both front ends share exactly the same command handling, so they can never
disagree about what a command does.
Well? What do you want me to keep track of?
| `todo <description>` | Adds a task with no date attached. |
| `deadline <description> /by <d/M/yyyy HHmm>` | Adds a task due at a given time. |
| `event <description> /from <d/M/yyyy HHmm> /to <d/M/yyyy HHmm>` | Adds a task spanning a period. |
| `find <keyword> [more keywords]` | Shows tasks matching any of the keywords. |
| `mark <number>` / `unmark <number>` | Marks a task done or not done. |
| `snooze <number> <days>` | Pushes a deadline back by a number of days. |

Alice is a task manager for people who would rather type than click. She keeps
track of your todos, deadlines and events, remembers them between runs, and is
faintly put out about having to do any of it.
She is not especially gracious about it - the replies below are verbatim -
but every message still tells you exactly what happened.

Alice saves to `data/alice.txt` after every command that changes anything, and
reloads it when she starts. There is no save command; it just happens.

a line in the file cannot be read - because it was hand-edited, say - she skips
that line, keeps the rest, and tells you which one she skipped.

This indirection exists because of a JavaFX packaging quirk: when the

* Launching from a separate class with an ordinary {@code main} method
* avoids that check, while {@link Main} still does the real JavaFX setup.

fx:root (rather than a plain <HBox> tag) is required here because
DialogBox.java calls FXMLLoader.setRoot(this) before loading: the
loader needs to be told what type the already-constructed root object
is, instead of being asked to instantiate a new one.
